items.explanation: In the first decades of contact, Native peoples did not quickly adopt European livestock. Horses and cattle spread gradually and were taken up widely only much later; the book notes Native peoples were initially terrified of the mounted Spaniards. Disease, missionary activity, and the transfer of American crops to Europe all began almost immediately.
options: A. Epidemics that devastated Native communities
B. The rapid adoption of horses and cattle by Native peoples
C. Missionary efforts to convert Native peoples to Catholicism
D. American crops such as maize and potatoes reaching Europe
items.stem: In the decades after 1492, contact between Spaniards and Native Americans produced all of the following EXCEPT

option_explanations.A: This did happen: the exchange of diseases across the Atlantic caused devastating epidemics among Native peoples, who had no immunity to Old World pathogens. It is a real outcome, so it does not answer an EXCEPT question.
option_explanations.B: Correct. In the decades right after 1492, Native peoples did not rapidly adopt European horses and cattle. Livestock spread slowly and reached most Native groups only decades later — Plains peoples, for example, became horse-mounted cultures in the 1600s and 1700s. This is the one listed outcome that did not occur.
option_explanations.C: This did happen: missionaries — Franciscans, Dominicans, and others — traveled with or close behind the conquistadors and began trying to convert Native peoples almost immediately.
option_explanations.D: This did happen: the Columbian Exchange carried American crops such as maize, potatoes, tomatoes, and tobacco to Europe within decades of contact.

items.explanation: Sugar cultivation was brutally labor-intensive, and the Native workforce had been shattered by conquest and especially by European diseases. With too few laborers available, colonists began importing enslaved Africans, starting in the 1540s.
options: A. The region had few inhabitants when Spaniards arrived
B. Native workers lacked knowledge of sugar cultivation techniques
C. Aztec and Inca rulers had already established the slave trade
D. Sugar harvesting demanded far more workers than were available
items.stem: Colonists in the Western Hemisphere turned to enslaved African labor chiefly because

option_explanations.A: The region was not empty: tens of millions of people lived in the Americas when Europeans arrived, and the early colonial labor force was in fact Native. The problem was that this workforce was collapsing, not that it never existed.
option_explanations.B: Knowledge of sugar-growing was not the obstacle. Europeans introduced sugarcane to the Caribbean themselves; what they ran short of was laborers, because Native populations were being destroyed by conquest, overwork, and above all disease.
option_explanations.C: The Aztec and Inca empires did not create the transatlantic slave trade. The enslavement and shipment of Africans across the Atlantic was a system built by European colonists and merchants, beginning in the 1540s in the Spanish colonies.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Harvesting sugarcane was extremely labor-intensive, and the Native labor supply had collapsed. With far too few workers available, colonists began importing enslaved Africans to do the work.

items.explanation: North American Native societies ranged from the urban mound-builders of Cahokia to Pueblo farming villages to nomadic hunting bands of the Plains and Great Basin. No single description fits them all.
options: A. They shared a largely uniform way of life
B. They copied the social models of Mesoamerican empires
C. They varied widely in lifestyle and economic organization
D. They routinely united in alliances against rival tribes
items.stem: Which statement best describes Native American societies in North America before sustained European contact?

option_explanations.A: There was no single shared way of life. A fishing village on the Pacific coast and a Mississippian farming town had little in common, so a uniform description cannot be right.
option_explanations.B: North American societies were not copies of Mesoamerican empires. The Aztec and Mexica states lay far to the south; peoples in what is now the United States and Canada developed their own distinct economies and social orders.
option_explanations.C: Correct. North American Native societies ranged from large settled farming towns like Cahokia to Pueblo villages to mobile hunting bands on the Plains and in the Great Basin — no single description fits them all.
option_explanations.D: Intertribal warfare did occur, but there were no routine, continent-wide alliances of tribes against one another. Alliances were local, temporary, and driven by specific rivalries, not a general system.

items.explanation: The voyages were financed by ambitious monarchs like Ferdinand and Isabella and driven by profit, religious zeal, and better ships and instruments such as the caravel, astrolabe, and compass. Europe was not democratizing; royal power was growing stronger.
options: A. Pursuit of wealth and new markets
B. The spread of Christianity
C. The rise of democratic government in Europe
D. Advances in ships and navigation
items.stem: Which of the following did NOT help drive European expansion into the Western Hemisphere?

option_explanations.A: The search for wealth — gold, silver, spices, and new markets — was a real driver of the voyages; Columbus sailed seeking a trade route, and conquistadors followed reports of treasure.
option_explanations.B: Religious zeal was a real driver: Spaniards framed their expeditions partly as spreading Catholic Christianity, and missionaries sailed with the conquerors.
option_explanations.C: Correct — this is the exception. Fifteenth-century Europe was not becoming democratic. Power was concentrating in monarchs like Ferdinand and Isabella, who personally sponsored the voyages.
option_explanations.D: New maritime technology was a real driver: the caravel, the astrolabe, and the magnetic compass let Europeans sail beyond coastal waters for the first time.

items.explanation: The first Americans migrated across the Bering Strait thousands of years before 1492 and lived mainly as mobile hunter-gatherers following fish and game, settling into farming villages only much later and only in some regions.
options: A. Moved seasonally following food sources
B. Built permanent towns and cities
C. Practiced settled agriculture exclusively
D. Arrived only a few centuries before 1492
items.stem: The earliest peoples of the Americas

option_explanations.A: Correct. The first Americans were mobile hunter-gatherers who moved seasonally following fish and game, having crossed from Asia thousands of years before 1492. Settled farming developed only much later, and only in some regions.
option_explanations.B: Permanent towns and cities did not exist among the earliest arrivals. Large settlements such as Cahokia came thousands of years later, after agriculture developed.
option_explanations.C: The earliest peoples practiced no agriculture at all, settled or otherwise — they hunted and gathered. This option reverses the sequence entirely.
option_explanations.D: They arrived far earlier than a few centuries before 1492 — roughly 15,000 or more years ago, across the land bridge from Asia.

items.explanation: Cortes's Second Letter (1520) was written to Charles V after Cortes defied his superior, Governor Velazquez of Cuba, to launch the Mexico expedition. Scenes of toppling 'idols' and preaching 'but one God' present a legally dubious private venture as faithful service to God and king -- exactly the framing Cortes needed to win retroactive royal approval.
options: A. Its portrayal of the expedition as loyal service to crown and church
B. Its scrupulous neutrality between Spanish and Aztec perspectives
C. Its criticism of the Spanish crown's colonial policies
D. Its argument that Native peoples should govern themselves
items.stem: The fact that this letter was addressed to Charles V best helps explain which feature of the document?
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"In these chapels are the images or idols... the principal ones, in which the people have greatest faith and confidence, I precipitated from their pedestals, and cast them down the steps of the temple, purifying the chapels in which they had stood, as they were all polluted with human blood, shed in the sacrifices. In the places of these I put images of our Lady and the Saints... I answered, through the interpreters, that they were deceived in expecting any favors from idols, the work of their own hands... and that they must learn there was but one God, the universal Lord of all, who had created the heavens and earth, and all things else, and had made them and us."
—Hernando Cortés, Second Letter to Charles V, October 30, 1520 (abridged)

option_explanations.A: Correct. Cortés wrote this letter to Charles V after launching the Mexico expedition against the orders of his governor, Velázquez of Cuba. Presenting the campaign as the destruction of idols and the preaching of 'but one God' cast an unauthorized venture as loyal service to God and king — exactly the case Cortés needed to win retroactive royal approval.
option_explanations.B: The letter is not neutral: it is written from a triumphalist Spanish Catholic point of view, celebrating the casting down of Aztec 'idols' and the imposition of Catholic images. There is no balance between the two perspectives.
option_explanations.C: Cortés criticizes no royal policy here; his whole aim is to win the king's favor, not to question how the crown ran its colonies.
option_explanations.D: Cortés argues nothing like self-government for Native peoples. The letter assumes Spanish authority over them — he is reporting his own actions as the king's agent.

items.explanation: Cortes entered Tenochtitlan in 1519 with only a few hundred Spaniards. He survived by exploiting resentment of Aztec domination -- most importantly the Tlaxcalan alliance -- and by the shock effect of steel swords, gunpowder, and horses, advantages no Aztec army could match. Disease would later ravage the city during the 1521 siege.
options: A. A Spanish field army that greatly outnumbered the Aztec forces
B. The Aztec Empire's lack of any organized system of warfare
C. Indigenous alliances against Aztec rule, combined with steel weapons, horses, and firearms
D. The conversion of the Aztec priesthood to Christianity before 1520
items.stem: Which of the following best explains how Cortes's few hundred men were able to carry out the actions described in the passage?
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"In these chapels are the images or idols... the principal ones, in which the people have greatest faith and confidence, I precipitated from their pedestals, and cast them down the steps of the temple, purifying the chapels in which they had stood, as they were all polluted with human blood, shed in the sacrifices. In the places of these I put images of our Lady and the Saints... I answered, through the interpreters, that they were deceived in expecting any favors from idols, the work of their own hands... and that they must learn there was but one God, the universal Lord of all, who had created the heavens and earth, and all things else, and had made them and us."
—Hernando Cortés, Second Letter to Charles V, October 30, 1520 (abridged)

option_explanations.A: The Spanish were not more numerous — the opposite. Cortés had a few hundred men against an Aztec Empire of millions, so numbers cannot explain his success.
option_explanations.B: The Aztecs did have an organized system of warfare, with trained warrior ranks and a record of conquering neighboring city-states. Cortés's advantage was not facing an unmilitary society.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Cortés's small force survived and won by allying with peoples who resented Aztec domination — above all the Tlaxcalans — and by the shock value of steel weapons, firearms, and horses, which no Mesoamerican army could counter. Epidemic disease also crippled Tenochtitlan during the 1521 siege.
option_explanations.D: No mass conversion of the Aztec priesthood occurred before 1520. Christianization of Mexico came after the conquest, not before it.

items.explanation: Cortes's language -- toppling 'idols,' cleansing chapels 'polluted with human blood,' preaching 'but one God' -- carries the crusading idiom of the Reconquista, the centuries-long Christian reconquest of Iberia from Muslim rule that ended in 1492. The conquest of the Americas inherited that vocabulary of holy war against nonbelievers.
options: A. The Portuguese policy of peaceful coastal trading in Asia
B. The Reconquista, in which Christian rulers framed war against non-Christians as holy struggle
C. The Spanish Inquisition's persecution of conversos within Spain
D. Columbus's commercial search for a westward route to Asia
items.stem: Cortes's actions in the passage most directly continue which earlier Iberian tradition?
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"In these chapels are the images or idols... the principal ones, in which the people have greatest faith and confidence, I precipitated from their pedestals, and cast them down the steps of the temple, purifying the chapels in which they had stood, as they were all polluted with human blood, shed in the sacrifices. In the places of these I put images of our Lady and the Saints... I answered, through the interpreters, that they were deceived in expecting any favors from idols, the work of their own hands... and that they must learn there was but one God, the universal Lord of all, who had created the heavens and earth, and all things else, and had made them and us."
—Hernando Cortés, Second Letter to Charles V, October 30, 1520 (abridged)

option_explanations.A: Portugal's Asian empire was built on fortified coastal trading posts and commerce, not on wars of religious conquest against non-Christians — it is a different Iberian model from what Cortés is doing.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Cortés's language — casting down 'idols,' cleansing chapels 'polluted with human blood,' preaching 'but one God' — speaks the crusading idiom of the Reconquista, the centuries-long Christian reconquest of Iberia that concluded in 1492. The conquest of the Americas inherited that tradition of holy war against nonbelievers.
option_explanations.C: The Inquisition's targets were conversos and others inside Spain suspected of heresy — an internal religious-purity campaign, not the older tradition of outward holy war that Cortés's language draws on.
option_explanations.D: Columbus's 1492 voyage was a commercial gamble seeking a westward trade route to Asia, not an act of religious warfare; it does not match the holy-war framing of this passage.
